Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe techniques and indications for arthroscopy of the ankle and surrounding structures.
Review common pathologies managed via ankle arthroscopy and important anatomic and
surgical considerations.
Discuss the outcomes of ankle arthroscopy and compare them with those of open surgery.
Procedure
Overview
Thorough knowledge of the anatomy of the foot and ankle is required for safe and successful
ankle arthroscopy.
Ankle arthroscopy aids in identifying and managing several pathologies of the joint space and
surrounding areas, including impingement, loose bodies, arthritis, synovitis, ankle instability,

The workhorse portals for anterior ankle arthroscopy are the anteromedial and anterolateral
portals. Accessory posterior portals, immediately adjacent to the Achilles tendon or the
peroneal tendon, can be used for posterior access.
For posterior ankle arthroscopy, the workhorse portals are created in the posterolateral and
posteromedial hindfoot on either side of the Achilles tendon.
Small joint arthroscope and instruments (Figure 1)
2.5-mm/2.7-mm/4.0-mm, 30°, and rarely 70° arthroscope
4.0 mm, especially for more extensive bone work (eg, large osteophytes, arthrodesis), allows
for a larger field of view
2.9-, 3.5-, or 4.0-mm shaver blades may be used, depending on the extent of pathology and
joint access, with tighter joint spaces potentially requiring smaller and/or curved
instrumentation.
3.5-, 4.0-, and 5.0-mm burrs may be used, depending on the extent of bony work, with 4.0-
mm and 5.0-mm burrs for arthrodesis. For impingement surgery, a hooded burr helps
protect anterior soft tissues.
Ring curettes, angled chondral picks, and microvector drill guide may be available alone or as
part of a commercially available ankle arthroscopy instrumentation system.

Noninvasive ankle distraction system
A noninvasive ankle strap and metal distractor (Figure 2) versus waist distraction (Figure 3);
the metal distractor is helpful for lesions that are more difficult to access, such as posterior
osteochondral lesions.
Optimizing distraction may be helpful in avoiding malleolar osteotomies.
Placement of the ankle in distraction and in a plantarflexed position allows for improved
access to the middle and posterior talar dome lesions as necessary.
Figure 2 Intraoperative photograph shows a noninvasive ankle strap and metal distractor for
ankle arthroscopy. After the patient is prepared, a sterile, noninvasive distractor is placed
over the dorsal midfoot and around the posterior heel and tensioned to bring the ankle into
a plantarflexed position. (Reproduced from Digiovanni BF, Kohring JM: Arthroscopy of the
ankle, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1157-1166.)

General Indications
Arthroscopy is a less invasive approach to access and correct pathology of the ankle and
posterior hindfoot joints. The goal of arthroscopy is the same as that of any surgical
procedure: identify and manage pathology to reduce pain and/or improve function.
Arthroscopy also is a valuable diagnostic tool.
Ankle and hindfoot arthroscopy is used to manage several pathologies. The specific surgical
approach (anterior, posterior) often depends on the location and severity of the deformity.1
Common indications for ankle arthroscopy are listed in Table 1.
Table 1 Common Indications for Ankle Arthroscopy
Distal fibula fractures
Loose bodies (in/around ankle joint)
Ankle arthritis
Subtalar arthritis
Arthrodesis
Synovitis
Lateral ankle instability

Osteochondral defects

Sinus tarsi syndrome
Endoscopic management of the Achilles tendon
Ganglion cyst
Courtesy of Dominic Carreira, MD, Alpharetta, GA.

General Indications
The ability to access the appropriate locations for the necessary treatment options is the
primary concern. For example, anterior ankle impingement is managed via anterior
portals, whereas os trigonum is managed via a posterior or lateral approach. In some
patients, such as those with osteochondral lesions of the talus, specific localization of the
injury site (anterior/central/posterior, lateral/central/medial) will inform the surgical
approach. Arthroscopic-assisted open surgery (such as open reduction and internal
fixation) also has been described and is particularly useful for identifying and managing
osteochondral defects, loose bodies, deltoid interposition, and syndesmotic instability.
General Contraindications

Broadly speaking, contraindications to ankle arthroscopy primarily are related to the following:
Limited joint access, such as large osteophytes
Inability to provide appropriate management, such as severe deformity in ankle arthritis
related to arthroscopic fusion
Active local infection that extends beyond the joint
Poor vasculature
Fractures more appropriately managed via open reduction and internal fixation (this
procedure may be performed with arthroscopic assistance)

General Contraindications
Arthroscopy is a tool for orthopaedic surgeons to correct ankle pathology, reduce pain,
and improve function. Arthroscopy may be considered based on the nature of the injury,
surgeon experience and skill, equipment limitations, evidence to support specific
treatment options, and patient comfort level.
Preoperative Planning
Preoperative planning for ankle arthroscopy should include an extensive review of relevant
patient history, symptoms, physical examination findings, and imaging findings.
Radiographs for ankle injuries typically include weight-bearing AP, oblique, and lateral views.
CT
CT scans may be useful in preoperative planning for ankle arthroscopy, particularly with
regard to identification of bone alignment in patients with a fracture, spurring in patients
with impingement, and the bony component of osteochondral and arthritic changes.
MRI
In the context of ankle arthroscopy, MRI may be helpful in assessing primary and associated
pathologies, such peroneal injuries in patients with ankle instability. Surgeons must correlate
imaging studies with clinical findings and patient symptoms because, occasionally, MRI may
reveal pathology that is not contributing to patient pain.
Anterior Ankle Arthroscopy

Overview
Appropriate patient positioning and noninvasive distraction are keys to efficient and successful
anterior ankle arthroscopy.
Setup/patient positioning
The patient is placed in the supine position. If the patient is taller than 6 ft,3 in, then an
extension may be added to the foot of the table to allow for the application of noninvasive
distraction.
Padding used to bump the surgical hip above the contralateral limb
A thigh leg support is used, and the knee is flexed to 45° (Figure 4), with care taken to keep
the popliteal fossa free of pressure.
Figure 4 Intraoperative photograph shows anterior setup for ankle arthroscopy, with the
patient in the supine position. (Courtesy of Dominic Carreira, MD, Alpharetta, GA.)
The thigh leg support is attached to the table at the level of the midthigh. A thigh tourniquet
typically is used. The heel should rest just off the surgical table (Figure 5). If the thigh support
is attached proximal to the distal leaf of the surgical table, the foot up and down control of
the table can be used to adjust traction after metal distraction has been attached.
Waist distraction facilitates manipulation of the joint and ease of access on entering the joint
space (Figure 5) and is particularly useful in managing impingement.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:20 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004002

Figure 5 Intraoperative photograph shows patient positioning for ankle arthroscopy. The
patient is placed in the supine position on a flat-top table, and a thigh tourniquet is placed.
The surgical leg is placed in a thigh support leg holder with padding under the posterior
thigh. The foot should barely touch the table, with the knee resting in a flexed position.
(Reproduced from Digiovanni BF, Kohring JM: Arthroscopy of the ankle, in Lieberman JR, ed:
AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1157-1166.)
Portal Placement
Primary portals for anterior ankle arthroscopy include the anteromedial and anterolateral
portals.
The anteromedial portal is established first, and subsequent portals are created under direct
visualization.
An accessory posterior portal may be established, if necessary, to manage more posterior
lesions.
Anteromedial Portal
The anteromedial portal is placed just medial to the tibialis anterior tendon and just lateral to
the medial malleolus in the soft spot at the level of the tibiotalar joint (Figure 6). The use of a
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:20 AM
AAOS | Ankle Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004002
8/46

22-gauge needle to inject the ankle joint with saline or an anesthetic containing epinephrine
helps identify the correct portal location and distends the joint to facilitate placement of the
arthroscope.
Figure 6 Intraoperative photograph of a foot and ankle shows the location of the anteromedial
ankle portal (arrow) for arthroscopy. Note that portal placement is a fair distance away from
the medial malleolus and close to the medial course of the tibialis anterior tendon. This
position ensures that visualization is not obscured by the medial malleolus. (Reproduced from
Digiovanni BF, Kohring JM: Arthroscopy of the ankle, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive
Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp
1157-1166.)
The most common error with anteromedial portal location is placement too far medially. If this
occurs, the medial malleolus blocks full manipulation of the arthroscope and compromises
joint visualization.
The structures most at risk during anteromedial portal placement are the greater saphenous
nerve and the saphenous vein. The use of a small hemostat to bluntly dissect soft tissue at the
SEND FEEDBACK

portal site in a longitudinal direction allows for free passage of instruments without entrapping
neurovascular structures (Figure 7).
Figure 7 Intraoperative photograph of an ankle shows blunt dissection with the use of a
hemostat. (Courtesy of Dominic Carreira, MD, Alpharetta, GA.)
Anterolateral Portal
The anterolateral portal is placed at the level of the ankle joint, medial to the lateral malleolus
and in the soft spot just lateral to the peroneus tertius tendon (Figure 8).

Figure 8 Intraoperative photograph of a foot and ankle shows the position of the anterolateral
ankle portal. This portal is located proximal to the tip of the fibula and approximately 5 to 10
mm proximal to the anteromedial portal. (Reproduced from Digiovanni BF, Kohring JM:
Arthroscopy of the ankle, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1157-1166.)
The portal is made under direct visualization with the arthroscope in the anteromedial portal.
A needle aids in atraumatic identification of an appropriate position parallel to the tibiotalar
joint surface and is used as a temporary outflow. The needle can be used as a proxy for access
to pathology, particularly in the management of osteochondral lesions.
The most common error with anterolateral portal location is placement too far distally.
The structure at greatest risk during placement of the anterolateral portal is the intermediate
dorsal cutaneous branch of the superficial peroneal nerve (SPN; Figure 9). Damage to the SPN
is the most common iatrogenic complication of ankle arthroscopy. Extreme care and precision
are necessary in establishing the anterolateral portal, with identification of the SPN if possible.

Figure 9 Illustration shows the surface anatomy of the lower leg. Note the course of the
superficial peroneal nerve and its distal branches. Because of the branching pattern, the
intermediate dorsal cutaneous branch of the superficial peroneal nerve is at risk of injury
during anterolateral portal placement. (Reproduced from Stetson WB, Ferkel RD: Ankle
arthroscopy: I. Technique and complications. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1996;4[1]:17-23.)
Identify and label the SPN via plantarflexion and inversion of the fourth toe. This is the nerve
most at risk during this procedure on establishment of the anterolateral portal (Figure 10).
Transillumination of the anterolateral skin via the arthroscope can help identify the crossing
nerve branches.

Figure 10 Intraoperative photograph of an ankle shows the superficial peroneal nerve.
(Courtesy of Dominic Carreira, MD, Alpharetta, GA.)
Posterolateral (Accessory) Portal
The posterolateral portal is optional and used to improve visualization of the posterior third of
the tibiotalar joint. It may be established for arthrodesis, posterior osteochondral lesions,
visualization, or outflow.
The posterolateral portal is placed approximately 2 cm proximal to the tip of the lateral
malleolus and immediately lateral to the Achilles tendon. It also is one of the main portals
used in posterior arthroscopy.
A 22-gauge needle can be used to identify the correct location while the arthroscope is in the
anteromedial portal for visualization. Another option is to place a switching stick (a smooth
metal rod) in the anteromedial portal. The switching stick is inserted through the capsule, and
the cannula is placed over the rod through the posterolateral portal. In a tight joint, this will
not be possible.
The structures at greatest risk during placement of the posterolateral portal are the sural
nerve and the lesser saphenous vein.
Video 1 shows setup and diagnostic examination for anterior ankle arthroscopy. In this video,
a thorough assessment of the joint space is performed via anteromedial, anterolateral, and
posterolateral portals. In this video, the posterolateral accessory portal was established before
the anterolateral portal, which is unusual. The anterolateral portal typically is the second

Diagnostic Ankle Arthroscopy

Diagnostic Ankle Arthroscopy
Ankle arthroscopy may be indicated as a supplementary tool for various acute or chronic
conditions. Chronic lateral ankle ligament injuries rarely occur in isolation, and a high
incidence of concomitant intra-articular and extra-articular pathology has been reported.
Intra-articular pathology, such as soft-tissue impingement lesions, osteophytes, loose
bodies, synovitis, and osteochondral lesions of the talus, frequently can be managed
arthroscopically. Therefore, many surgeons routinely perform ankle arthroscopy in
combination with lateral ankle ligament repair or reconstruction.2 Bare and Ferkel3
performed diagnostic ankle arthroscopy in combination with open peroneal tendon
repair in 30 patients and found intra-articular pathology in 100% of the patients (most
commonly scarring but also synovitis, osteochondral lesions, loose bodies, and ligament
damage).

Common Anterior Arthroscopic Treatment Options
Anterior Ankle Impingement
Bony and soft-tissue impingement of the anterior ankle may result from the following:
Chronic joint synovitis, including in the setting of a previous ankle fracture
Ankle instability
Repeated loading and dorsiflexion of the ankle (especially during sports)

Anterior Ankle Impingement
The clinical presentation includes anterior ankle pain, typically worse in dorsiflexion. The
physical examination may reveal pain with palpation of the anterior ankle joint,
especially in a dorsiflexed position. Bony impingement may be visualized on plain lateral
radiographs. MRI may aid in determining articular cartilage involvement, which is
important in predicting the likelihood of surgical success.
Syndesmotic impingement refers to soft-tissue impingement of the anterolateral ankle
joint at the site of the syndesmotic ligaments. Injury to the ankle syndesmosis may result
in persistent pain and dysfunction secondary to syndesmotic impingement. This injury
often involves the anterior tibiofibular ligament, with resulting synovitis and scarring
along its length.
Arthroscopic management of syndesmotic impingement involves débridement of the
synovitis and scarring at the anteroinferior tibiofibular ligament, with removal of the
Bassett ligament, if present. Only approximately 20% of the syndesmotic ligament is
intra-articular.4 If the syndesmotic complex is competent, excision of this portion, if
necessary, will not cause mechanical problems (Figure 11).

Syndesmotic Injury

Syndesmotic Injury
The syndesmosis of the ankle consists of three anatomic structures: the anteroinferior
tibiofibular ligament, the posteroinferior tibiofibular ligament, and the interosseous
membrane. In patients with a severely displaced ankle fracture, in addition to
management of articular cartilage damage, arthroscopic evaluation and management of
the syndesmosis, including postreduction assessment of the syndesmosis from inside
the joint, may be indicated. In addition, evaluation of medial clear space widening and
any potential deltoid interposition may be advantageous in assessing for suspected
injuries to the syndesmotic complex.
Controversies in distal tibiofibular syndesmotic injury and arthroscopic-assisted fixation
are discussed in Video 6.

Controversies in Foot and Ankle Trauma. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, San Diego, CA, March 14-18, 2017.
Clinical Evaluation
Clinical tests and imaging studies can aid in determining the extent of the injury. A midcalf
squeeze test (Hopkin test) and ankle dorsiflexion with external rotation may produce
syndesmotic pain. The length of tenderness along the lateral ankle also is an indicator of injury
severity. In patients with syndesmotic disruption, plain radiographs may demonstrate the
following signs:
Increased tibiofibular clear space
Decreased tibiofibular overlap
Increased medial clear space
Considerations for syndesmotic pathology are discussed in Video 7.

Synovitis

Synovitis
Inflammation of the synovial lining of the ankle may lead to generalized hypertrophic
synovitis. Pain and nonspecific swelling throughout the joint may have several causes,
including rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, crystalline disease, or infection. Additional
pathologies include benign synovial hyperproliferative diseases, such as pigmented
villonodular synovitis, and synovial chondromatosis. Localized areas of synovitis may be
noted in patients with traumatic injury, such as sprains, and/or with repetitive overuse.
Synovitis is readily managed via arthroscopic débridement, synovectomy, and joint
irrigation. Minimally invasive management often is advantageous. Joint aspiration and
fluid analysis are indicated if septic arthritis is suspected. Regarding diagnosis, synovitis
may be difficult to identify because of the diffuse nature of symptoms and the
nonspecific clinical presentation. MRI may aid in identifying signal abnormalities near the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:20 AM
AAOS | Ankle Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004002
22/46

synovium. Surgical management, consisting of partial synovectomy and management of
associated pathology, including resection of adhesions, often is effective in providing
good relief of pain in patients with overuse, trauma, or inflammatory arthropathy.
In patients with pigmented villonodular synovitis or synovial chondromatosis, removal of
loose bodies in combination with synovectomy and débridement typically is an effective
treatment option. An attempt should be made to identify areas of extension beyond the
joint; in such patients, open surgical treatment also should be considered. Figure 13
shows diffuse synovitis of an ankle joint, which reddened and inflamed. Inflammation
from synovitis is easily visualized via arthroscopy, and it often occurs in combination with
other pathologies of the joint space, such as impingement.
Figure 13 Arthroscopic image shows diffuse synovitis of the ankle joint, which is
reddened and inflamed. Inflammation from synovitis is easily visualized via arthroscopy
and often occurs in combination with pathologies of the joint space, such as
impingement. (Courtesy of Dominic Carreira, MD, Alpharetta, GA.)
Osteochondral Defects


Osteochondral Defects
Ankle arthroscopy aids in the diagnosis and surgical management of osteochondral
lesions of the tibiotalar joint. Depending on the extent of the osteochondral defect,
management may consist of arthroscopy alone or arthroscopic-assisted management.
Arthroscopy permits access and visualization that typically is superior to that associated
with an open procedure. In most patients, nonsurgical treatment will not provide
substantial long-term pain relief, and surgical treatment is indicated, particularly in
patients with larger, unstable, and/or displaced fragments.
The general goals of arthroscopy in the management of osteochondral lesions include the
following:
Débridement of loose tissue, inflammation, loose bodies
Thorough assessment of the joint space, with identification of defects
Management of the defect (débridement only, microfracture, or grafting, depending on the
size)
Talar Dome Lesion

Talar Dome Lesion
The location and extent of the defect are important considerations (Figure 14).
Controversy exists with regard to the optimal management of osteochondral defects
because many treatment options are available, with little evidence of superiority across
techniques. For defects smaller than 1.5 cm2, microfracture of the area of the defect may
be appropriate.
Microfracture procedures include the following:
Involves punching tiny holes (microfractures) in the subchondral bone of an osteochondritis
dissecans lesion; this introduces bone marrow access to the chondral lesion, which leads to
clotting in the area of the defect.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:20 AM
AAOS | Ankle Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004002
24/46

Promotes localized neovascularization and migration of multipotent mesenchymal stem cells
to the osteochondritis dissecans lesion site
Induces repair rather than true native chondral regeneration; primarily produces type I
cartilage and does not result in native hyaline cartilage, which primarily is type II cartilage.
Relies on remaining intact cartilage as an anchoring point for multipotent marrow-derived
cells to adhere and repair the defect.
Management of osteochondral defects via microfracture involves the following steps:
Establishment of portals based on clinical and radiographic evaluation of osteochondral
defects (often anteromedial or anterolateral, but varies by patient)
Débridement of soft tissues and degenerated cartilage with the use of a shaver, burr, or
curet and removal of loose bodies
Removal of the base layer of cartilage, also known as the tide
Drilling into subchondral bone via a pick or an awl at different angles (30°, 45°, 90°) spaced
approximately 2 to 3 mm apart
Verification of marrow-derived elements and influx to the lesion site

Arthritis

Arthritis
Arthritis is the term used to describe diffuse articular cartilage damage of a joint rather
than localized areas of damage (i.e., osteochondral defects). The primary options for the
management of ankle arthritis include ankle fusion and ankle replacement.
Arthroscopic Arthrodesis
Arthroscopic ankle arthrodesis is a minimally invasive surgical technique for patients with ankle
arthritis (Figures 15 and 16). Compared with open fusion, limited evidence shows improved
vascularity, lower infection rates, faster fusion rates, less blood loss, and shorter hospital length
of stays. An arthroscopic approach may facilitate future conversion to ankle arthroplasty.
Suggested indications (in patients with arthritis) include the following:
Pain despite nonsurgical management
Adequate bone stock

Tendoscopy is a minimally invasive alternative for evaluation and débridement of the Achilles
tendon, posterior tibial tendon, flexor hallucis longus (FHL) tendon, and peroneal tendon.
Overview
Appropriate patient positioning, use of small joint arthroscope and small joint arthroscopic
instruments, and noninvasive distraction are keys to efficient and successful posterior ankle
arthroscopy.
Setup/Patient Positioning
The patient is placed in the prone position on a flat-top surgical table. The surgical leg is
bumped above the level of the contralateral limb for ease of access.
Portal Placement
Workhorse portals for posterior ankle arthroscopy include posterolateral and posteromedial
portals. These portals are located immediately adjacent to and on either side of the Achilles
tendon, extending 1 cm proximal to the tip of the lateral malleolus.
Depending on the pathology involved, a vertical adjustment to the level of the pathology can
be made via fluoroscopy, especially with subtalar fusions, to optimize the angle across the
posterior facet and enhance access to the ankle joint (Figure 18).

Posterolateral Portal
In posterior ankle arthroscopy, the posterolateral portal typically is the first access point
established (van Dijk technique). Its location is the same as that for an accessory portal for
anterior arthroscopy: lateral to the Achilles tendon, medial to peroneal tendons, and
approximately 1 cm proximal to the tip of the lateral malleolus.

spread technique), and blunt dissection (mosquito clamp) then should be performed to avoid
injuring the sural nerve.

same path when inserting the arthroscope.
Close proximity to the Achilles tendon reduces the risk of iatrogenic complications, especially
related to the location of the sural nerve.

Common Posterior Arthroscopic Treatment Options
Posterior Ankle Impingement

Posterior Ankle Impingement
Posterior ankle impingement frequently is caused by repetitive overuse injury, and is
most prevalent in high-activity athletes, such as dancers, football players, and runners.
Plantar flexion, rather than dorsiflexion, typically is painful. Therefore, the diagnosis
typically is based on clinical testing, with forced plantarflexion causing pain. This test
involves brief passive hyperflexion forces with slight internal and external rotation.
Radiography may aid in diagnosis by demonstrating an os trigonum or posterior talus
process deformity or fracture. In addition, MRI may aid in making the diagnosis.5
Arthroscopic management of posterior ankle impingement includes débridement of
inflamed tissues; identification of FHL pathology, including tenosynovitis or
tendovaginitis (narrowing); resection of loose bodies or fracture fragments, if present;

Arthroscopic Subtalar Arthrodesis

Arthroscopic Subtalar Arthrodesis
Arthroscopic subtalar arthrodesis is indicated in patients with arthritis and may be
indicated in the management of subtalar tarsal coalition or other arthritic conditions of
the subtalar joint. An arthroscopic approach is contraindicated if performing distraction
arthrodesis or if correction of a large deformity is required. The advantage of
arthroscopic arthrodesis is preservation of the talar and calcaneal blood supply, given
that the interosseous ligament and its associated vasculature are preserved. This
technique can be performed with the patient in the supine, lateral, or prone position;
however, the prone position for the posterior approach has increased in popularity and
is preferred by the authors of this lesson. Fusion rates are between 91% and 100%, and
time to union ranges from 6 to 12 weeks postoperatively. The advantages of the
arthroscopic technique include shorter hospital stays and decreased incidence of wound
complications and sural nerve injuries. Using the two standard posteromedial and
posterolateral portals, the surgeon resects the articular cartilage with the use of
curettes, osteotomes, and burrs. The remaining steps of alignment of the subtalar joint

Haglund Deformity

Haglund Deformity
For management of some conditions, such as Achilles tendinopathy or Haglund
deformity, the patient can be placed in the supine position—with the foot of the bed
dropped off and with the use of a posterior thigh holder and the foot hanging—or in the
prone position. A posterolateral portal is placed immediately proximal to the superior
margin of the calcaneus bone and immediately adjacent to the Achilles tendon.
The typical posteromedial and posterolateral portals are shifted inferiorly to facilitate
access to posterior calcaneus (Figure 19). A nick-and-spread approach is most
appropriate for protection of the sural nerve. A blunt trocar may be used to access and
expand the retrocalcaneal space. The posteromedial portal is established symmetric to
the posterolateral portal on the opposite side of the Achilles tendon and under direct
visualization. Débridement with the use of a 4.0-mm shaver is appropriate for removal of
bursitis and pathogenic tendon, if present. After débridement, the posterior calcaneal
prominence and the Achilles tendon insertion can be observed. Resection of the
Haglund prominence from the posterosuperior calcaneus is then performed with the
use of a burr or other tool. Care is taken to protect the Achilles tendon; if excessive
tendon is released from its insertion, tendon repair can be performed. Successful
resection is confirmed by assessing posterior impingement via dorsiflexion and lateral
fluoroscopy.

Additional Arthroscopic Approaches
Additional portals have been described in the arthroscopic or endoscopic management of
ankle and hindfoot pathology. Depending on the location of the pathology, access may be
restricted by joint space, bone structure, or simply the anatomy of the working space, which
indicates that additional portals may be more appropriate. Some portals located on the lateral
side of the ankle permit access to a series of additional structures, including the peroneal
tendons and the lateral ligaments of the ankle and subtalar joint.

Tips, Tricks, and Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Complete the surgical setup for arthroscopy before making an incision. After the incision is
made, bleeding occurs, and visualization becomes limited.
The use of a tourniquet and distension and infiltration with saline or an anesthetic mixed with
epinephrine are suggested. With experience, these measures may not be necessary.
Secondary portals usually are created under direct needle localization.
A fluid pump and alternating portals to optimize visualization and access often are helpful.
The size of the camera may be adjusted based on the extent of the pathology, with a 4.0-mm
arthroscope providing a larger field of view and greater flow than a 2.7-mm arthroscope.
Complications
Complications can be minimized via a detailed understanding of anatomy, the use of a nick-
and-spread technique, and the use of contemporary noninvasive distraction and surgical
techniques.
The incidence of iatrogenic damage to articular cartilage is estimated to be 31%, Iatrogenic
articular cartilage damage is related to chondral damage on creation of arthroscopic portals
during blunt dissection or subsequent procedures.
In a 2018 review, Zekry et al7 analyzed 55 studies and found complication rates ranging from
3.4% to 9%, with different considerations for anterior and posterior arthroscopy.
Anterior arthroscopy complication rates include the following:
SPN damage (or branches): 1.04% to 8.3%
Deep peroneal nerve damage: 0.2% to 0.77%
Saphenous nerve damage: 0.16% to 3.3%
Sural nerve damage: 0.08% to 4.04%
Superficial infection: 0.13% to 3.3%

Extensor hallucis longus rupture: reported in three studies
Extensor digitorum communis rupture: reported in one study
Postoperative swelling: 0.3%
Complex regional pain syndrome: 0.1%

Complications
Complications in foot and ankle arthroscopy commonly include transient
nerve/sensation loss or infection, with serious complications reported at a rate of 1.1%.
With anterior arthroscopy, the most common complication is neurologic injury, with
approximately one-half of these injuries involving the SPN (approximately 4%
complication rate for SPN damage). Other neurologic concerns may be related to the
distraction or nerve blocks. With the advent of noninvasive distraction and refined
surgical techniques, these risks are mitigated; however, limiting time in distraction is an
important consideration.
With posterior arthroscopy, the sural nerve is the structure most at risk for iatrogenic
damage, with the incidence of sural nerve dysesthesia ranging from 0.08% to 4.04%. To
decrease the risk of nerve irritation, the surgeon should limit the amount of time the
ankle is distracted. Transient Achilles tendon tightness is the most common complication
of posterior arthroscopy, resulting in complication rates as high as 4.1% and possibly
higher. Blood thinners, elevation, and progression via physical therapy can decrease the
risk of deep vein thrombosis (0.08% to 0.4%), which is most relevant during the initial
immobilization period.
A synovial cutaneous fistula is more common with ankle arthroscopy than with
arthroscopy of other joints. A short period of immobilization is recommended (5 to 7
days) to decrease the incidence of draining fistula formation.

Outcomes

Outcomes
Arthroscopic management of ankle joint pathology has been well studied and generally
results in long-term outcomes comparable with those of open procedures. Depending
on the location, type, and extent of pathology, arthroscopy may be appropriate. With
regard to the outcomes of patients who underwent arthroscopy for the management of
ankle impingement, Zwiers et al9 reported good to excellent results in 74% to 100% of
patients, with 94.3% to 97.5% of patients reporting that they would undergo the
procedure again. For anterior impingement, arthroscopy is the preferred treatment
option for bone and soft-tissue injury. Arthroscopic débridement provides adequate
relief of painful or function-limiting pathology in a manner superior to that of open
treatment options with regard to technical access and patient outcomes.
In patients who underwent ankle arthrodesis, Woo et al10 reported that arthroscopic
minimally invasive surgery was associated with shorter recovery, less pain, and fewer
complications. Several other studies on arthroscopic fusion suggested faster bony union
and superior achievement of clinical milestones compared with open procedures.11-13
High success rates are achieved, even in patients who undergo concurrent lateral
ligament repair. Xu et al14 reported comparable clinical outcomes in patients who
underwent open or arthroscopic treatment for osteochondral lesions during lateral
ligament stabilization. Across all arthroscopic procedures, reduced rates of infection and
decreased recovery time and scarring are general trends relative to open procedures.
Results of posterior arthroscopy and hindfoot endoscopy are comparable to those of
open procedures, with some evidence suggesting reduced recovery time and less
morbidity with minimally invasive management of posterior impingement and with
subtalar fusion. General trends persist regarding achievement of results comparable
with those of open procedures, and results are especially favorable with fusion.15,16

In general, posterior arthroscopy results in good outcomes with minimal complications.
In a study of 146 arthroscopic hindfoot procedures for the management of FHL
tendinitis, bony impingement, and osteochondral defects, van Dijk and van Bergen17
reported that most patients had good outcomes. In a study comparing open
retrocalcaneal decompression and arthroscopic management, Leitze et al18 reported
that the procedures resulted in similar American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society
outcome scores and comparable recovery times. In a study of 12 athletes who
underwent arthroscopic treatment for posterior bony impingement, Noguchi et al19
reported a substantial increase in American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society scores
and range of motion, with a mean time to return to sports activity of 6 weeks.
Frey et al20 reported good or excellent outcomes in 94% of patients who underwent
subtalar arthroscopy. Most patients in this cohort who had sinus tarsi syndrome also
had interosseous ligament damage or rupture at the time of surgical treatment,
suggesting that subtalar arthroscopy allowed for a more specific diagnosis and more
accurate assessment of hindfoot joint pathology. Similar findings were reported by Lee
et al21 in a cohort of 31 patients (33 cases) with sinus tarsi who underwent subtalar
arthroscopy. In 29 of the 33 cases (88%), the talocalcaneal interosseous ligament was
damaged. Clinical outcome scores (American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society scores)
were meaningfully improved after arthroscopic débridement, with good to excellent
results reported in 87% of the cases.
